case_study_insert.main_stem: Ridgeline Quarry Aggregates (RQA) is a private limited company in the crushed-stone extraction sector in the Scottish Highlands, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2008 by Fiona Ridgeline, it supplies road-building aggregate to regional contractors and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. RQA plans to invest $920,000 in a new mobile stone-crushing and screening plant with low-dust eco-technology, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $320,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.50 a unit and a selling price of $14.50, and produces 100,000 units a year. RQA faces two problems: dust complaints from nearby residents have risen and the defect rate for off-specification aggregate has reached 4.2%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The crushing line dispatched 24,000 tonnes of aggregate last quarter at an off-specification defect rate of 4.2%, up from 2.6% a year earlier. Dust complaints from residents rose from 9 to 17 per month. Average lorry turnaround is 42 minutes. Market research of 500 local contractors found that 68% would pay up to $0.50 more per tonne for low-dust, recycled-content aggregate, and 57% check environmental credentials before ordering. A skills audit shows 16 of 52 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new screening plant; accredited off-the-job courses at the technical college cost $950 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Ridgeline Quarry Aggregates for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, the fifth rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.00 to $13.75 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills at labour-intensive quarry sites. (3) Wholesale diesel, steel wear-part and recycled-feedstock costs have risen 11.2% year-on-year, construction-cost inflation is 6.4%, and regional road-building orders grew 2.8% over the same period.

questions.question_text: RQA plans to fund part of its $920,000 crushing-plant expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for RQA of using $320,000 retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit is internally generated, so RQA pays no interest and makes no loan repayments on the $320,000 used for the $920,000 crushing plant. With fixed costs of $300,000 a year and a $600,000 bank loan already committed, avoiding extra debt service protects cash flow and the $6.00 contribution on each unit sold. Every dollar saved can instead fund dust-suppression equipment to address the 17 complaints a month recorded in the operations report.

Point 2: Using retained profit keeps control with Fiona Ridgeline and the existing owners, because no lender can impose conditions or repossess the mobile screening plant if demand from regional contractors disappoints. It also avoids disclosing sensitive quarry data to outsiders while the 4.2% off-specification defect rate is being tackled. Retained profit is flexible: it can be drawn in stages as the low-dust plant is commissioned, unlike a bank loan which must be drawn and serviced on fixed dates. That flexibility matters in a seasonal road-building market where 24,000 tonnes were dispatched last quarter and cash may arrive unevenly from contractors.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to RQA's financing decision, costs and operational problems.

questions.question_text: RQA wants to win new road-contractor contracts for its low-dust aggregate. Consider national trade-press advertising, local radio sponsorship, or a social media campaign aimed at contractors. Which should RQA choose to promote the new crushing plant? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National trade-press advertising: Adverts in road-construction and quarrying magazines reach exactly the regional contractors that buy RQA's crushed stone. The low-dust, recycled-content message can be backed with technical data, and the research showing 68% of 500 contractors would pay $0.50 more gives a clear premium story. Trade press carries credibility with procurement staff and has a long shelf life. However, lead generation is slow and production costs are significant for a business already committing $920,000 to new plant.

Local radio sponsorship: Sponsoring regional traffic or farming programmes is cheaper and gives rapid, repeated exposure around the quarry's catchment, which suits a time-limited message that the new screening plant is online. Yet the audience is broad and largely not the specifiers of aggregate. RQA sells to contractors rather than the general public, so much of the spend is wasted, and the 57% of surveyed contractors who check environmental credentials are unlikely to be reached in a buying context.

Social media campaign: Targeted posts on professional platforms can show dust-monitoring results and recycled-content credentials to procurement managers at low cost with measurable engagement. They can explain how the new low-dust plant addresses the rise from 9 to 17 complaints. Nevertheless, contractors in this market still rely on established supply tenders and personal relationships, so online interest may not convert into the large tonnage orders needed to utilise 100,000 units of output.

Recommendation: RQA should choose national trade-press advertising. It reaches the specialist buyer, carries the technical credibility needed to justify the $0.50 premium, and supports the tender relationships that radio cannot. Local radio is rejected as untargeted and wasteful for a specialist industrial product; social media is rejected as cheap but unlikely to convert into the high-volume contractor contracts needed to fill the $920,000 plant. A small social media presence can reinforce the trade press message afterwards.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of promotional options with minimal application to RQA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of RQA with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of RQA with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and social media are rejected.

questions.question_text: RQA's dust complaints have risen from 9 to 17 a month and its hierarchical structure relies on autocratic leadership. Explain two benefits for RQA of involving its workforce of 52 more democratically.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A more democratic style gives RQA's 52 workers a voice in how the new low-dust screening plant is operated, which can raise satisfaction and reduce the absenteeism that disrupts a 24,000-tonne quarterly dispatch schedule. Quarry operators see dust at the face first-hand, so their suggestions on water spraying and machine settings can cut the 17 complaints a month more effectively than top-down instructions from an autocratic manager.

Point 2: Consulting workers builds commitment to quality, helping lower the 4.2% off-specification defect rate and the 2.6% figure it rose from. Staff who help design inspection routines are more likely to follow them, protecting the $14.50 selling price and the reputation needed to win contractor tenders. Higher involvement can also reduce labour turnover, saving the $950 per employee cost of accredited courses for the 16 of 52 staff still needing training on the plant, and making the $920,000 investment pay back more smoothly.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RQA's complaints, defect rate, training needs and output.

questions.question_text: RQA must train 16 of its 52 workers to operate the new screening plant. Consider on-the-job training on the crushing line or accredited off-the-job training at the technical college. Which should RQA choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Instruction at the crushing line is specific to RQA's own screening plant and dust-control routines, costs no course fees, and keeps the 16 workers productive while they learn, protecting the 24,000 tonnes dispatched last quarter. Trainers can demonstrate exactly how to avoid the 4.2% off-specification defect rate. Drawbacks are that experienced operators lose time while coaching, bad habits may be passed on, and there is no external certificate, which could matter if contractors ask for evidence of competence.

Off-the-job training: The accredited technical-college course costs $950 per employee, so 16 workers cost $15,200 in total — small beside the $920,000 plant. It provides structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised qualification that supports contractor tenders, while removing staff from noisy quarry conditions. However, it takes workers off the line, reducing short-term capacity when dust complaints are already 17 a month, and the generic syllabus may not match RQA's exact low-dust settings, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: RQA should choose on-the-job training as the main method, with short college modules later for the most senior operators. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing output at a time when absenteeism and complaints are already problems. Full off-the-job training is rejected because taking 16 of 52 workers away would threaten dispatch schedules and its generic content would still require on-site adaptation; the $15,200 is better spent later once the plant is stable. RQA can also keep the 24,000-tonne quarterly dispatch on schedule while coaching happens on the line, and accredited modules can be added later for senior operators without losing momentum against the 17 dust complaints.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to RQA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of RQA.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how RQA's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $300,000 ÷ ($14.50 − $8.50) = $300,000 ÷ $6.00 = 50,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 50,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $14.50 − $8.50 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways RQA's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 50,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 100,000 units to confirm the quarry is comfortably profitable, giving a margin of safety of 50,000 units before the new plant's extra fixed costs would be at risk.
2. Use the $6.00 contribution per unit to model pricing: if contractors won the $0.50 a tonne premium identified by research, contribution would rise to $6.50; managers can judge whether discounting to win tenders still covers $300,000 of fixed costs.
3. Set output targets for servicing the $600,000 bank loan: 50,000 units covers fixed costs, so each additional unit adds $6.00 toward interest and repayment on the $920,000 investment.
4. Benchmark unit cost ($300,000 ÷ 100,000 units + $8.50 = $11.50 a unit) each quarter to spot the cost of the 4.2% off-specification defect rate and the 11.2% input-cost inflation in Appendix 3.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 50,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 100,000 units; premium-pricing and discount modelling around $300,000 fixed costs; loan-service volume targets for the $920,000 plant; and unit-cost benchmarking at $11.50 to track defects and inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RQA's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and return on capital employed (ROCE) for 2024 and 2025. Has RQA's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: Gross profit 1,920 ÷ revenue 4,800 × 100 = 40.0% in 2024; 2,430 ÷ 5,400 × 100 = 45.0% in 2025. Operating profit 576 ÷ revenue 4,800 × 100 = 12.0%; 810 ÷ 5,400 × 100 = 15.0%. Operating profit 576 ÷ capital employed 3,200 × 100 = 18.0%; 810 ÷ 3,600 × 100 = 22.5%. Revenue rose from 4,800 to 5,400 while cost of sales increased only from 2,880 to 2,970, so gross profit widened from 1,920 to 2,430. Capital employed grew from 3,200 to 3,600 as the $920,000 plant was commissioned, and interest expense rose from 64 to 72.

Evaluation: Every one of the three measures moved favourably, so the improvement is broad rather than the result of one figure. The widening gap between revenue and cost of sales suggests RQA gained pricing power, consistent with contractors valuing low-dust aggregate, and operating profit grew faster than revenue, showing good control of overheads despite higher interest expense. Returns on the larger capital base also improved, meaning the new asset is already contributing. A caution is that the $920,000 plant is only just commissioned, so 2025 may not yet reflect its full running costs, and the 4.2% defect rate and rising dust complaints could push costs of sales up in future years.

Conclusion: RQA's profitability has clearly improved. Gross and operating margins and returns on capital all rose together, so the judgement is well supported; management should now protect the gain by cutting the defect rate and securing the $0.50 premium before cost inflation erodes it.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States isolated financial figures with little or no accurate calculation of the three measures.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three measures for both years with some contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of revenue, cost, capital and interest movements and a justified conclusion on profitability.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RQA of using low-dust eco-technology and recycled-content aggregate in its new crushing plant.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The research shows 68% of 500 contractors would pay up to $0.50 more per tonne for low-dust, recycled-content aggregate, and 57% check environmental credentials before ordering. Using the low-dust plant lets RQA charge that premium, protecting the $6.00 contribution per unit against the 11.2% input-cost inflation and helping justify the $920,000 investment. It also directly tackles the 17 dust complaints a month, reducing the risk of local opposition to quarry operations.

Disadvantage: Low-dust equipment and recycled feedstock can be more expensive to buy and operate than conventional crushing, which would raise the $8.50 variable cost per unit and squeeze the margin unless the full $0.50 premium is accepted across all 100,000 units. Recycled-content material may also vary in quality, which could push the current 4.2% off-specification defect rate higher and increase waste before operators master the new screening plant, undermining the very environmental credentials the strategy is meant to sell.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RQA's research data, costs and defect rate.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in input costs will affect RQA. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): If RQA's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point increase adds 0.0075 × $600,000 = $4,500 a year (shown derivation). That is modest beside fixed costs of $300,000 a year, and if the loan is fixed-rate the extra cost is zero. Higher rates may still make future borrowing for the $920,000 plant more expensive and could dampen the 2.8% growth in road-building orders.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, from $13.00 to $13.75 an hour): RQA employs a workforce of 52 at labour-intensive quarry sites, so this rise feeds into wage bills and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked and no individual pay rates, so no annual wage total can be honestly calculated; the correct approach is qualitative, judged against labour productivity of 100,000 units ÷ 52 workers = 1,923.1 units per worker (arithmetic shown from insert figures). Productivity must hold or output rise, or unit labour costs will climb and squeeze the $6.00 contribution from the $14.50 selling price less $8.50 variable cost.

Input cost inflation (11.2%): The insert does not decompose the $8.50 variable cost, so only an explicitly labelled upper bound can be computed: if the entire variable cost rose 11.2%, that is 0.112 × $8.50 = $0.952, about $0.95 a unit; across 100,000 units this is 100,000 × $0.952 = $95,200 a year. Even a smaller pass-through would materially reduce contribution, and the 6.4% construction-cost inflation makes price recovery harder, though the $0.50 premium backed by 68% of surveyed contractors offers partial protection.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It multiplies across all 100,000 units and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution that justifies the $920,000 plant, whereas the interest effect is a conditional $4,500 and the wage effect cannot even be quantified from the insert and can be offset by productivity. RQA should secure the premium and renegotiate feedstock contracts.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to RQA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on RQA's costs or financing in context with shown arithmetic where figures are used.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context, with derivations shown and a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact.
